thread.title: Look At Your ETF; It May Not Be What You Think It Is

author: Dave Dierking, CFA
title: Look At Your ETF; It May Not Be What You Think It Is
text:
In putting together model portfolios for my subscribers, I spend a lot of time digging into the details of the ETFs that ultimately make the cut. It's an absolutely necessary part of portfolio construction, because failure to do your due diligence can result in a portfolio that's not what you think it is. It can be overweight in certain sectors or styles or there may be significant overlap in holdings.
I started out my career working in the call center of a mutual fund company. I got to talk with a lot of people over time and it gave me some pretty interesting insights into the mind of the average investor. Most investors were performance chasers. They simply wanted to put their money into the best performing fund that year. People would frequently ask for "that 30% fund" or something like it. The lead-up to the tech bubble bursting was a particularly scary time watching unknowing investors piling their money into risky investments without having any idea of what they were buying (and thumbs down to the fund companies that shamelessly advertised huge returns in order to attract assets with little concern for the potential consequences).
I remember one lady calling in requesting information on our Growth & Income Fund, which happened to be a solid performer at the time. Then she added "and the Equity Income Fund for diversification." Her heart was in the right place, but she thought simply that more funds equaled more diversification. In reality, Growth & Income and Equity Income were virtually identical. They had the same portfolio manager. Eight of the top 10 holdings were the same. They both focused on large-caps. The only real difference was that Growth & Income was slightly more tilted towards growth, but there was significant overlap between the two portfolios and pairing them up offered almost zero additional diversification benefits.
This is just an example from 20 years ago, but it emphasizes the importance of knowing what you own and what you're buying. It's especially tricky nowadays with over 2,000 ETFs available to choose from. In a lot of cases, the ETF is legitimately doing what its objective sets out to do, so it's not like there's any nefarious intent, but the end result can be unexpected. Take, for instance, the new Innovation Shares NextGen Protocol ETF ( KOIN ), otherwise known as one of the blockchain ETFs introduced earlier this year. Take a look at the fund's website to see how the company describes its objective:
Innovation Shares NextGen Protocol ETF (KOIN): Blockchain is a new digital protocol for authentication and authorization that allows parties to bypass a centralized administrator. To give this basket a more defined framework, stocks are placed in one of four custom stakeholder categories in terms of how they relate to the theme: Cryptocurrency as Payment, Mining Enablers, Solutions Providers and Adopters.
Our ETF seeks to give investors access to companies that may benefit from a technology that has the potential to revolutionize the way global trade is conducted, data is secured, supply chains are managed, financial instruments are cleared and contracts are recorded.
This sounds legitimate enough. It's simply trying to identify the companies that are dedicating the most resources, both physically and financially, to blockchain development. But look at KOIN's top 10 holdings:
This is a good case of how a legitimate strategy produces an unintended consequence. These companies may be making the biggest investments in blockchain, but this looks a whole lot like a generic large-cap tech ETF. Given the fact that KOIN charges 0.65%, investors would probably be better off with something like the Vanguard Information Technology ETF ( VGT ) that charges just 0.10% and gives you similar coverage.
I don't mean to pick on this fund in particular, but it's a good reminder of why you should always know what you're investing in. KOIN is just a small fund, but this problem also arises in some of the biggest ETFs around. If you're looking to build the core of your portfolio using broadly diversified, ultra-low cost ETFs, the problem of portfolio overlap can become a BIG problem if you don't fully understand how each component works and what universe it's targeting.
Let me give you a real life example using the Vanguard funds. Let's say you want to construct a core U.S. equity portfolio and you're considering the following funds:
Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF ( VTI ) Vanguard Mega Cap ETF ( MGC ) Vanguard Large Cap ETF ( VV ) Vanguard Mid Cap ETF ( VO ) Vanguard Small Cap ETF ( VB ) Looking through the prospectus, each of these funds uses the CRSP US Total Market Index as its foundation. VTI uses the full index, while each of the four other funds uses a subsection of the index, so we know we're at least comparing apples to apples. Now, Vanguard also offers ETFs based on S&P and Russell indices. For example, in addition to VB, you could also choose the Vanguard S&P Small Cap 600 ETF ( VIOO ) or the Vanguard Russell 2000 ETF ( VTWO ). There are differences though between these funds as the names themselves would suggest. VIOO holds about 600 stocks. VTWO holds around 2000 names. VB? Around 1400. You might think that any of these three small cap ETFs is essentially interchangeable, but you'd be wrong. VB and VIOO, for example, actually have very little overlap.
Less than 20% of assets between these two small cap ETFs overlap. That's a significant difference. That's just one way two seemingly similar products are different, but let's get back to our original example to see another way.
Looking at its composition, VTI, according to Morningstar, is about 47% mega-caps, 30% large-caps, 17% mid-caps and 6% small-caps. Let's say that you want to maintain some flexibility and potentially tweak this asset allocation over time. Instead of investing 100% in VTI, you decide to put 47% in MGC, 30% in VV, 17% in VO and 6% in VB. Since they're all based off of the same starting index, you figure this is one of those "6 of one, half dozen of the other" situations. According to Morningstar, at least, they're pretty much identical portfolios, right?
Wrong!
Here's the not so fun part. You need to dig into the prospectus to find out why they're not the same thing, but here's the Cliffs Notes version. After applying some basic screens for things like size, liquidity and tradeability, eligible companies are sorted by market cap. Once sorted, cumulative market cap breakpoints are established, which essentially consist of the total market cap of all higher cap companies up to that point. For example, looking solely at the biggest component weights of the S&P 500, Apple ( AAPL ) would be the top 4.1% of total market cap, Apple plus Microsoft ( MSFT ) would be the top 7.4%, Apple plus Microsoft plus Alphabet ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ) would be the top 10.2%, and so on. So if a fund has an index range of 0-50%, it would include the largest companies that make up the top half of total market cap. Confusing enough? Hang with me.
Let's go back to the four Vanguard ETFs and see the market cap ranges they've been assigned:
See the problem? Those five indexes aren't unique. What CRSP defines as the large-cap index is actually a combination of the mega-cap and mid-cap indexes. How exactly they can justify putting a company in both a large-cap and a mid-cap index baffles me, but that's how they're doing it. An overlap analysis of the Mega Cap ETF and the Large Cap ETF confirms the doubling-up.
A full 83% of assets appear in both ETFs. If you were to buy the combination of MGC, VV, VO and VB in the percentages mentioned above, you'd be overweighting mega-caps and mid-caps and underweighting small-caps. If you wanted unique coverage, you would only want to use either the Mega Cap ETF/Mid Cap ETF combination or the Large Cap ETF to pair with the Small Cap ETF. I won't dive too far in the weeds here and run down more examples, but there are lots of others if you're willing to look. Schwab (NYSE: SCHW ), for example, has some complicated inclusion criteria for its large-, mid- and small-cap indexes so there is some overlap there too.
The differences can also be fairly pronounced in style or sector ETFs. If you take a look at two of the biggest momentum ETFs - the iShares Edge MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF ( MTUM ) and the Invesco DWA Momentum Portfolio ETF ( PDP ) - you'll find a lot of dissimilarities despite a seemingly similar approach. MTUM, for example, looks at excess returns over different periods in the past to determine momentum. PDP is a little more vague saying that it creates a momentum score for eligible securities that is based on "intermediate and long-term upward price movements of the security as compared to a representative benchmark index." It's a similar concept that delivers dissimilar results.
From a sector standpoint, these two funds are invested very differently. MTUM is up to more than 40% in tech, but PDP is under 30%. Investment in the industrial sector is also very different. MTUM is mostly large-caps, where PDP has nearly half of assets invested in mid- and small-caps. Put the two ETFs side by side and there is only a 19% overlap in total assets.
So how do you choose between the two funds in a situation like this? I think it's important to examine your risk preferences, your purpose in choosing the fund and how it fits into your existing portfolio. Sometimes, the way the portfolio is constructed can be a big differentiator. For example, if I were to choose a blockchain ETF to add to my portfolio, I'd choose an actively managed one since the industry is changing so quickly. I'd want a fund that can quickly respond to changes versus one that will only update itself twice a year. In choosing between the momentum ETFs, you could ask yourself if you're comfortable with a potentially riskier mid-cap fund over one focused on large-caps. MTUM is also much cheaper, which should be another important tiebreaker.
Conclusion Building a portfolio, unfortunately, isn't as simple as choosing funds with the right name. Even constructing a seemingly simple straightforward portfolio of core funds can cause issues. The lesson, as always, is to do your own due diligence. There are a lot of funds out there that look the same on the surface, but can be very different under the hood. Fortunately, a quick read of the "principal investment strategies" section of a prospectus can usually point you in the right direction. Reading legal disclosure in tiny font isn't anybody's idea of fun (at least it shouldn't be), but a little spent on it can go an awfully long way towards smart portfolio construction.
